newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: More poll protests begin in Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: More poll protests begin in Belgrade.

text.p: Serbia's opposition launched new protests on Friday aimed at forcing the authorities to block President Slobodan Milosevic's attempt to annul local election results which went badly against him.
Hundreds of students gathered outside the University of Philosophy around noon in the first of two major protests planned for the day.

Student leaders said they would join their rally with an opposition demonstration scheduled for 3 p.m. (1400 GMT) to protest "violation of basic democratic principles and unscrupulous trampling of elementary human rights".
Friday's protests marked the fifth day of demonstrations in Belgrade and towns across Serbia to demand that the results of local polls held last Sunday be recognised.
The opposition said it expected electoral commissions and courts to give their final rulings on Friday.

Leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition accuse the government of extensive fraud by annulling votes which gave the opposition sweeping victories in 15 of the 18 biggest towns in Serbia.

Milosevic's ruling Socialists conceded defeat in Belgrade and the northern town of Novi Sad, but in the industrial town of Nis turned a major defeat into victory after the local election commission ruled in their favour.
Some 20,000 people marched through Belgrade on Thursday, waving opposition party flags and flinging insults at Milosevic, in the city's biggest demonstrations for three years.
Zoran Djindjic, one of three opposition coalition leaders expected to become the new mayor of Belgrade, said protests would continue until the Socialists verified the poll results.
Students last took to the streets in the wake of 1991 demonstrations which Milosevic crushed with massive police force and tanks. Two men were killed.
The students then staged a round-the-clock sit-in in the centre of Belgrade, forcing him to make concessions.

"The tenacity and endurance of the demonstrations is sorely testing the authorities. The most alarming fact for them is that the numbers of demonstrators in Belgrade is growing instead of diminishing," one diplomat said.

Milosevic has already been warned by the United States to improve his poor human rights record if he wants to see the lifting of an "outer wall" of sanctions which bars Belgrade from desperately-needed foreign capital.
The United States and Britain have voiced grave concerns over the opposition's allegations.

On Thursday Britain's ambassador to Belgrade Ivor Roberts wrote to the Zajedno leaders saying he was concerned by "the uncertainty and allegations over the results of the Serbian municipal elections".

"I have personally conveyed our concerns to the authorities here at the highest levels," He wrote. "In particular I urged that any irregularities should be dealt with promptly and in accordance with the law."
Roberts said he had initiated an urgent discussion with the European Union, which was expected to issue a joint statement in Brussels.
Some tensions were likely to be defused by the reported return of the wife of opposition leader Vuk Draskovic.
Draskovic, who leads the Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO) in the Zajedno coalition, on Thursday accused the authorities of "kidnapping" his wife Danica -- a political figure in her own right.

On Friday an SPO official confirmed Danica had telephoned from her home to say she had been released and was safe and well. There was no independent confirmation of the alleged kidnapping and subsequent release.
